---
title: "Organic matter in water exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Two equal metal totals

Waters A and B each contain 2.00 µmol/L dissolved total metal. Free metal is 0.500 µmol/L in A and 0.100 µmol/L in B. Assume only free and organically complexed forms. Find bound fractions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Subtract free from total, then divide by total.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
A is **75.0% bound**; B is **95.0% bound**. The free-ion amounts differ by a factor of five despite identical totals. This simplified partition does not by itself give a toxicity endpoint.
:::

## 2. Oxygen inventory

In a sealed litre of water, oxygen starts at 9.00 mg/L. Completely oxidise 2.00 mg C/L of CH₂O-like substrate, with no other oxygen terms. Calculate residual O₂.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Demand is carbon mass × 32/12.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Demand = **5.33 mg O₂/L**; residual = **3.67 mg/L**. The calculation assumes the complete aerobic oxidation can occur and ignores gas exchange and competing processes.
:::

## 3. Incomplete degradation

Only 25% of a 4.00 mg C/L CH₂O-like pool is oxidised during an observation period. Calculate model oxygen consumption. Can you report it as the ultimate demand?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Apply the accessible fraction before the stoichiometric ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Oxidised carbon = 1.00 mg C/L, so consumption is **2.67 mg O₂/L**. Complete oxidation of the entire pool would require 10.67 mg O₂/L. The period-specific consumption is not the ultimate demand.
:::

## 4. Interpret a dark-water change

Water becomes darker while DOC changes little. What chemical explanations and measurements would you consider?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Carbon quantity and optical properties are different observables.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Changes in molecular composition, chromophoric groups, particle content, or iron-associated colour could alter absorption per unit carbon. Compare spectra/absorbance, DOC, filtration, iron, and pH. Do not infer a unique source, degradation rate, or toxicity from colour alone.
:::

## Explore: oxygen demand in a sealed bottle {#explore}

Predict how much of the ultimate oxygen demand of 4.00 mg C/L is used in a
5-day test, and whether 9.00 mg/L of oxygen is enough to oxidise all of it.
Change one input at a time.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="oxygen" role="group" aria-label="Oxygen demand of organic carbon in a sealed bottle">
<p>Reference case: 4.00 mg C/L has an ultimate demand of 10.67 mg O₂/L. With a rate of 0.10 per day, 4.20 mg O₂/L (39%) is used in 5 days, and a bottle starting at 9.00 mg/L runs out of oxygen on day 18.6.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/oxygen.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Exercise 2: sealed litre**. Check the ultimate demand and the
oxygen left after complete oxidation against your answer to exercise 2.

**E2.** Choose **Exercise 3: 5-day test**, then **Slow humic carbon**. The carbon
amount and ultimate demand are the same. Why does the 5-day result differ so
much, and what does that mean for a brown lake?

**E3.** Reset, then move the measurement day until about 25% of the demand is used.
Compare the oxygen used with your answer to exercise 3. Then move to day 40:
why does the oxygen used stop at 9.00 mg/L instead of reaching 10.67?

### Model conditions and hand check

Ultimate demand = carbon × 32.0/12.0. For 3.00 mg C/L this gives **8.00 mg O₂/L**;
for 2.00 mg C/L, **5.33 mg O₂/L**, leaving 9.00 − 5.33 = **3.67 mg/L**; for
4.00 mg C/L, **10.67 mg O₂/L**. With a first-order rate of 0.10 per day, the
oxygen used by day $t$ is $10.67\,(1-e^{-0.10t})$, which is 4.20 mg/L on day 5
and reaches 25% (2.67 mg/L) after about 2.9 days.

The organic matter is represented by CH₂O, so 1 mol C uses 1 mol O₂. The rate
constant is a constructed round value, not a measured property of any water.
The bottle is sealed and dark: no reaeration, no photosynthesis and no other
oxygen users such as nitrification. When the oxygen is used up the aerobic
model stops; reactions with other electron acceptors are not modelled.
